text: At a turn of the road, he saw the figure of a man, in grave and decent clothes, seated at the foot of an old tree, who rose and walked beside him. <break time="0.8s" /> You are late, Goodman Brown, said the stranger, for the clock of the Old South was striking as I came through Boston, and that is full fifteen minutes ago. <break time="0.8s" /> The traveler was about fifty years old and looked so much like Goodman Brown that they might have been taken for father and son. <break time="0.8s" /> The only thing about him that could be fixed upon as remarkable was his staff, which bore the likeness of a great black snake and seemed to wriggle like a living serpent. <break time="0.8s" /> Come, Goodman Brown, said the traveler, this is a dull pace for the beginning of a journey, so take my staff if you are so soon weary. <break time="0.8s" /> Friend, said the young man, stopping short, having kept my promise by meeting thee here, I now intend to return whence I came, for I have scruples about this business. <break time="0.8s" /> My father never went into the woods on such an errand, nor his father before him, said Brown, for we have been a race of honest men and good Christians. <break time="0.8s" /> The traveler replied that he had helped Browns grandfather whip a Quaker woman through the streets of Salem, and had helped his father burn an Indian village in King Philips War. <break time="0.8s" /> I have a general acquaintance in New England, he added, and the deacons of many a church, the selectmen of many a town, and even the governor are firm friends of mine.
